# Project 2: Localization [![tests](../../../badges/submit-proj2/pipeline.svg)](../../../pipelines/submit-proj2/latest)

#1. There are more particles within a 10cm radius in the noise-free model (fig. 2) because it does not take into account the noise that is generated by the system which can lead to errors. The fig. 2 plot assumes it is a perfect system: it has perfect sensors that don't make mistakes and have infinite resolution, the motors respond perfectly to applied voltage and the battery always has a perfect output. Since fig. 3 takes into account all these noises from the real world and assumes what could go wrong with the system numerically, it obviously presents more possibilities spread out in the map.


#2. My initial parameters, the particles were spread far apart and did not form a consistent banana-shaped distribution compared to Figure 3.  To reduce the excessive spread, I decreased delta_std from 0.5 to 0.1.  In MM2, the banana-shaped distribution was more concentrated with 20 out of 100 particles within 10cm of the mean.  We are resembling closer to Figure 3 but the spread in the y axis is slightly larger.  I decided to further reduce the positional and heading noise to improve the distribution for MM3. Compared to Figure 3, the final plot maintained a similar banana-shaped trajectory, although the particles were distributed somewhat differently along the curve. The final result had 15 out of 100 particles within 10 cm of the mean, compared to 21 out of 100 in Figure 3.

#3. The drawbacks of the conditional independence assumption is not true, the belief of the state of the car is dependent on both the sensor and motion models, both have valuable information on where is the current state of the car. We mitigate this drawback with the Bayes rule, as it takes both of these seemingly independent inputs and combines them to have a dependent probabilistic model. The resulting distribution emphasizes measurements consistent with the expected distance while still accounting for unexpectedly short readings, maximum-range measurements, and random sensor noise.

#4. The initial model produced a narrow Gaussian peak around the expected LiDAR distance which does not account for much uncertainty.  Increased the hit_std (standard deviation) therefore the Gaussian peak was lower but the distribution became wider.  I then increased z_hit to give more importance to measurements that closely match the expected distance.
